slides.title: The first Thanksgiving
text: In 1620 a ship called the Mayflower sailed from England to America. The passengers, called the Pilgrims, wanted a new life.
Their first winter was terrible. It was very cold and they didn't have much food. The Wampanoag people, who lived there, helped them. They showed the Pilgrims how to grow corn and where to fish.
In autumn 1621, after a good harvest, the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag shared a big meal. Today Americans remember this feast at Thanksgiving.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
paragraphs: It's Saturday morning and I'm not watching cartoons. I'm not playing football. I'm standing in my gran's hall with my arms around a big brown wardrobe, and the wardrobe is winning.
"Push, Tomás!" says Gran. "You're not hugging it. You're moving it!"

My name is Tomás. I'm eleven, I'm in the 6.º ano and I live in Graça, an old part of Lisbon with very steep streets. The yellow tram climbs our hill every day, and every day it complains. My gran, Avó Lurdes, lives two streets away from us, on the second floor of an old building with no lift. She's seventy-nine and she climbs the stairs faster than me.
The painters are coming on Monday, so Gran needs an empty hall. She also needs workers. That's me, my best friend Duarte and Ruby.

Ruby is new at our school. She's from Edinburgh, in Scotland. Her dad is Scottish and her mum is American, from Boston. Ruby's Portuguese is terrible, but she isn't shy. Every week she learns a new word and uses it a hundred times. This week's word is "fixe". The canteen soup is fixe. Maths is fixe. Nobody agrees with her about maths.

Now everybody is working. Duarte is sweeping the floor, but he's eating a biscuit at the same time, so he's making more crumbs than he's sweeping. Ruby is putting old books into boxes. Gran is standing in the middle of the hall like a football coach. She isn't working. She's giving orders.
"Duarte, you're sweeping, not dancing! Ruby, those are my cookbooks, not rubbish! Tomás, why are you sitting down?"
"I'm not sitting down, Avó. I'm resting standing up."

On Saturday mornings, Gran sits in her armchair, drinks a small black coffee and listens to the radio. She always sings with the old songs, very loudly and very badly. Today she isn't sitting and she isn't singing. She's nervous, and I don't know why.
Ruby holds up a blue scarf. "Senhora Lurdes, is this yours?" she asks in English.
"No, it isn't mine. It's my sister's," Gran answers. In English. Perfect English.
Ruby's mouth opens. "Wow! Your English is brilliant! Where did you learn it?"
Gran's face closes like a door. "From letters," she says, and she walks into the kitchen.
Duarte looks at me. I look at Duarte. My gran speaks English? Since when?
"Come on," I say. "One, two, three!"
We push. The wardrobe moves, it shakes, and something falls from the top: an old tin box. It hits the floor, the lid opens and suddenly there are postcards everywhere.

Ruby picks one up. "Look! It's Edinburgh Castle! That's my city!" On the postcard, the castle is sitting on its big black rock. Duarte finds a bridge with two tall towers over a river. "Tower Bridge, London," he reads. There's a castle in Cardiff, the capital of Wales, and a big white building with a green dome: City Hall, Belfast. They all end with the same words: "Your friend forever, Peggy."
"Who's Peggy?" asks Duarte.
"Those are mine."
Gran is standing in the doorway with a tea towel in her hand. She isn't smiling. "Give them to me," she says. "Now, please."
We give them to her. She puts them back in the tin, carries it into her bedroom and closes the door. Then we hear a key. She's locking it.

We push the wardrobe again, quietly this time. It moves to the middle of the hall, and behind it, on the dusty floor, there's one more postcard. The picture shows a big square next to the river, Praça do Comércio, with a yellow tram in front of the arch. There's no stamp on it.
I turn it over. The writing is small and round. Ruby reads it aloud, slowly:

"Dear Lurdes, Yesterday I waited for you at the top of your hill for two hours. Where were you? My ship is leaving tonight. I've got a present for you, but it's too big for your door, so Mr Costa at Casa Costa, Rua da Madalena, is keeping it for you. Please go and get it. Your friend forever, Peggy. 13 August 1966."
"1966?" says Duarte. "That's sixty years ago! My grandad was a baby!"
"So your gran never got her present," says Ruby. "She never saw this postcard. It was behind the wardrobe all this time."
I think about Gran's face and her locked door. "We can't show it to her now. She's upset."
"Then we find the present first," says Ruby. Her eyes are shining. "Then we give her the postcard and the present together. It's perfect!"

Duarte is already typing on his phone. "Casa Costa, Rua da Madalena... It still exists! Look: antiques, clocks and music boxes." Then his face changes. "Oh no. Closing down. Everything must go. Last day: 31 October."
"Then we're going there on Monday," says Ruby.
I put the postcard in my pocket. My heart is beating very fast. Behind me, a door opens.
"Tomás," says Gran quietly. "What have you got in your pocket?"

chapters.title: Everything Must Go
paragraphs: "My phone," I say.
It's a lie. My phone is in my other pocket. Gran looks at me for a long time. Then she goes back into her bedroom without a word. I feel terrible. I never lie to Gran. Well, almost never.

On Monday after school, the three of us are standing at the tram stop in Largo da Graça. The 28 is coming down the street, yellow and noisy, and it's full of tourists. Everybody is holding a phone, and everybody is taking photos of the same old houses.
We get on. It's very crowded, and a man with a huge backpack is standing on Duarte's foot.
"Excuse me," says Duarte. "I need that foot. I'm a goalkeeper."

The tram goes down through Alfama. The streets are so narrow that the tram almost touches the walls, and there are clothes hanging from every window: shirts, socks, a pink dressing gown. The driver rings the bell at every corner.
We get off in Rua da Conceição, and then we're lost. Ruby's map is turning round and round on her phone. There's a man selling roasted chestnuts at the corner.
"Excuse me," Ruby says in English. "Where is Rua da Madalena, please?"
The man smiles and points. "Go straight on. Turn left at the church. Casa Costa? It's on the right, opposite the bakery." In Lisbon, everybody knows everything.

Casa Costa is dark and quiet. The shop smells of dust and old wood. Clocks are ticking on every wall. There are old cameras, gramophones, dolls with glass eyes and, on a long shelf, music boxes of every colour. Over the till there's an orange sign: EVERYTHING MUST GO! 50% OFF!
Ruby goes straight to a gramophone. "How much is this?"
An old man comes out from behind a curtain. He's got a white moustache, and his glasses are on top of his head. "Two hundred and fifty euros. With the discount."
"Oh," says Ruby. "That's... very expensive."
This is Senhor Costa. He's closing the shop because he's tired and his knees hurt. I show him the postcard and I explain everything in Portuguese. Ruby nods as if she understands.
Senhor Costa reads the postcard twice. Then he takes an old black notebook from a drawer. "My father wrote everything down," he says. "Look."
I can read it: "12 de agosto de 1966. Caixa de música. Paga. Para a menina Lurdes Rocha. Aguarda." A music box, paid, for Miss Lurdes Rocha. Waiting.
"My father never threw anything away," says Senhor Costa. "He kept things for people in a special cupboard. He always said: people come back."
"So where is the cupboard?" asks Duarte.

Senhor Costa's face goes pale. "Ai, meu Deus. Last week a woman from the Feira da Ladra bought everything in that cupboard. Dona Fátima. Everything!" Then he adds something strange. "And you aren't the first. Last week a young American lady asked me about a music box from 1966."
Ruby, Duarte and I look at each other. An American lady?

On Saturday morning we're at the Feira da Ladra, the big flea market near the church of São Vicente. It's open on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and you can buy everything there, even keys without doors and doors without keys.
Dona Fátima's stall is under a big blue umbrella. And there, between a broken lamp and a pair of football boots, is a small wooden music box with two silver birds on the lid.
Dona Fátima opens it. A little tune comes out, slow and a bit sad. I know this tune. Gran hums it when she's cooking.
"How much is it?" I ask.
"Eighty euros."
"Eighty? Can you do forty?"
"Eighty. And be quick, querido. An American girl wants it too. She's coming back next Saturday with the money. The first person with eighty euros takes it home."

We count our money. I've got twelve euros fifty. Ruby has got fifteen euros. Duarte has got nine euros twenty, a button and an old bus ticket. That's thirty-six euros seventy. We need forty-three euros thirty more, in one week.

It's the busiest week of my life. This week Duarte is washing cars in our street every afternoon, for two euros a car. Ruby is walking Bolacha, the fat little dog of Senhora Amélia, Gran's neighbour across the landing. Bolacha hates walking, so Ruby is carrying her most of the time. I'm carrying shopping bags up the steps of Graça for old ladies, and they're paying me in coins and cake.
On Friday night we count the money on my bedroom floor. Eighty euros and thirty cents!
On Saturday we're at the market at half past seven. The sellers are opening their umbrellas and putting out their tables. We run to the blue umbrella.
The music box isn't there.
"Sorry, kids," says Dona Fátima. "She came at seven o'clock."
"Who?"
She points across the square. A young woman with red hair and a long green coat is getting on the 28 tram. In her hands, she's holding a small wooden box with two silver birds on the lid.

chapters.title: A Guest for Thanksgiving
paragraphs: "Run!" shouts Ruby.

We run. The tram is slow because the street goes up, and Duarte is fast because he's a goalkeeper and goalkeepers never give up. People are jumping out of our way. A dog is barking. An old man is shouting, "Cuidado!"
The tram stops. The doors are open. I'm almost there... and the doors close in front of my nose.

Through the window, the woman with red hair is looking at us. She looks surprised. She's holding the music box on her knees, very carefully, like a baby. Then the tram turns the corner, and she's gone.

November is grey and wet. I'm not sleeping well and I'm not eating much, and that's serious, because I usually eat like Duarte. The postcard is in a drawer in my bedroom. I can't give it to Gran without the present, and I can't look at her without feeling like a criminal.
Then, one day in the canteen, Ruby says, "My mum is inviting all of you to Thanksgiving."
"What's Thanksgiving?" asks Duarte. "Is there food?"

"Of course there's food! It's an American holiday on the fourth Thursday of November. Families get together and have a big dinner. It started with a harvest meal in 1621. Now Americans eat turkey, watch American football and say what they're thankful for." She rolls her eyes. "American football isn't real football. It's people jumping on people."

So on the fourth Thursday of November, we're at Ruby's flat: me, my mum, Gran and Duarte. The flat smells wonderful. Ruby's dad is mashing potatoes and singing a Scottish song. Ruby's mum is taking an enormous turkey out of the oven. Ruby is putting the plates on the table, and Duarte is "helping": he's tasting everything.
"Senhora Lurdes, this is your seat," says Ruby. "And this one is mine. Duarte, that chair isn't yours, it's my dad's! Yours is next to Tomás."

Gran is wearing her best blue dress. She's talking to Ruby's mum in English, and they're laughing like old friends. My mum is trying to speak English with Ruby's dad, and he's trying to speak Portuguese with her. It isn't working, but they're both smiling.
There's turkey and mashed potatoes, sweet potatoes, green beans and a red sauce made with cranberries.
"Red jam with meat?" whispers Duarte. "Americans are crazy." Then he tries it, and he has three spoonfuls.
Ruby's mum looks at the clock. "We've got one more guest. She's a student from Boston, and she's alone in Lisbon this year. Nobody eats alone on Thanksgiving. That's the rule."
The doorbell rings. Ruby opens the door.
Red hair. Long green coat.
Duarte chokes on his cranberry sauce.
"Hi! I'm Claire," says the woman. "Sorry I'm late, the tram was full." Then she looks at us, and her eyes get bigger. "Wait. I know you three. You were running after my tram!"
Everybody looks at us. My face is as red as the cranberry sauce.

After the turkey, Ruby's mum stands up. "Now everybody says what they're thankful for." Ruby's dad is thankful for the Lisbon sunshine. Duarte is thankful for the turkey. Gran is thankful for her grandson, "even when he has got secrets in his pockets." She looks at me. I look at my plate.

Then it's Claire's turn. "I'm thankful because I found something for my grandmother," she says. "Sixty years ago, she came to Lisbon on a ship to meet her best friend. They were pen pals. They wrote letters for years, but they never met. My grandmother waited for her friend for two hours, and her friend never came. So she left a present for her in a shop." Claire takes something out of her bag. "I'm sending it to Boston on Monday."
It's the music box with the two silver birds. She opens it, and the slow, sad tune fills the room.
Gran puts down her fork very slowly. Her face is white.
"Play it again," she whispers.
Claire looks at her, confused, but she closes the box and opens it again. The tune starts again. Gran's lips are moving. She knows every note.
"What is your grandmother's name?" asks Gran. Her voice is shaking.
"Margaret Walsh. But everybody calls her Peggy. When she was a girl in Belfast, she was Peggy Byrne."
Gran stands up so fast that her chair falls over.
"That's impossible," she says. "Peggy Byrne is dead. She died in 1967."

chapters.title: Gone Away
paragraphs: Nobody ate the pumpkin pie that night.

For a moment, the room was completely silent. Claire was confused. Ruby's mum was still holding the gravy. Duarte had a potato on his fork, and it stayed there, in the air. My mum was holding Gran's arm.
"Dead?" said Claire. "No! My grandmother isn't dead. She's seventy-nine and she's very much alive. Last month she shouted at a taxi driver in Boston."
Gran sat down again, slowly. "But in 1967 I wrote to her in Belfast, and my letter came back. On the envelope there were two words in red ink: GONE AWAY."
Ruby's mum put down the gravy. "Oh, Lurdes. 'Gone away' doesn't mean dead. The post office writes it on a letter when the person moved house."
Gran looked at her. Then she laughed and cried at the same time. "Sixty years," she said. "Sixty years because of my terrible English!"

Claire explained the rest. In 1967, Peggy's family moved from Belfast to Boston. Her father wanted a new life in America. Peggy was twenty, and she was sad, because she never heard from her friend in Lisbon again.

Then I did a brave thing, or maybe a stupid thing. I took the old postcard out of my jacket and put it on the table in front of Gran. "I found this behind your wardrobe, Avó. In September. I'm sorry. I wanted to find the present first."
Gran read it. She read it again. "The top of my hill," she said quietly. "She waited for two hours." After that, she didn't say anything for a long time.

Claire closed the music box and gave it to her. "It's yours," she said. "It was always yours." Inside the lid there was a small envelope. On it, in small round letters, were the words: "For Lurdes. Open it when we meet. P."
Gran didn't open it. "When we meet," she said. "Not before."
December was strange. Christmas came, and Gran was quiet. Claire gave her Peggy's phone number, and Gran put it on her fridge with a magnet. She looked at it every day, but she never called.
"Why don't you call her?" I asked one evening.

"Because she didn't come," said Gran. "I was there, Tomás. On 12 August 1966, I waited at the top of the hill, at the castle, from four o'clock until seven. I was nineteen, and I was wearing my best dress. She wasn't there."
But Peggy's postcard said the same thing. She was at the top of the hill too. So who was wrong?

January was cold and wet. It rained for eleven days without stopping. The streets of Graça were like rivers, and the tram was always late. On Saturday, Duarte played in a football match in the rain. He jumped for the ball, slipped in the mud and landed on his ankle.
My mum is a nurse, so she looked at it in our kitchen. "What's the matter?" she asked.
"My ankle hurts. A lot."
"It isn't broken," she said. "But you need ice and rest. No football for three weeks."
Duarte looked at her as if she said "no food for three weeks".
At school, our English teacher, Teacher Sofia, gave us a project. "Write a biography," she said. "Choose a person from the past. When was he or she born? Where did they live? What did they do?"
I chose Peggy, of course.
So on a rainy Saturday, Ruby, Duarte and I met Claire at the pastelaria near Gran's flat. Duarte arrived last, on crutches. He ordered two pastéis de nata. "For my ankle," he explained.

Claire told us about her grandmother. Peggy was born in Belfast in 1947. Her father was a sailor. She was the fastest runner in her school. When she was eleven, her teacher started a pen-pal project with a school in Lisbon, and Peggy received a letter from a girl called Lurdes. They wrote to each other every month for eight years.
"In 1966," said Claire, "Grandma travelled to Lisbon on her father's ship. She walked to the top of Lurdes's hill. The hill in the photo."
"What photo?" I asked.
Claire took out her phone. "Grandma keeps this on her fridge in Boston. It's the only photo of Lurdes she has."

It was an old black and white photo. A girl of about twelve, with two long plaits, was standing next to a small white chapel. Behind her, there were pine trees and all of Lisbon: the river, the roofs and the castle on its hill. Under the photo, in a child's handwriting, there were three words: "O meu monte."
Ruby looked at it for a long time.
"Tomás," she said slowly. "Look. The castle is behind her, far away. Your gran isn't standing at the castle. She's on a different hill."

chapters.title: The Wrong Hill
paragraphs: We ran to Gran's flat in the rain. Duarte didn't run. He jumped on his crutches and complained all the way. "I'm the slowest detective in Lisbon!"
Gran looked at the photo on Ruby's phone, and she put her hand over her mouth.

"Senhora do Monte," she whispered. "My hill. I sent her this photo when I was twelve. My father took me there every Sunday." She sat down. "In 1966 I didn't think about the photo. Peggy was a foreigner, and foreigners always go to the castle. So I went to the castle." She looked out of the window. "From the castle walls, you can see Senhora do Monte. I was looking at her hill all afternoon, and she was looking at mine."
Then Gran stood up and put on her coat. "I want to go there," she said. "Now."
"Avó, there's a storm!"
"I'm seventy-nine. I'm not afraid of a little rain."

It wasn't a little rain. It was the worst storm of the winter. The wind was strong and cold, the rain was heavy, and water ran down the steep streets like a river. Gran walked up the hill faster than all of us. At the top, the miradouro was empty. The pine trees were moving in the wind, and the city below was grey.
Gran went to the old stone wall behind the benches. She touched the stones slowly, one by one. Then she stopped.
There, under the green moss, there were small letters and numbers, scratched into the stone a long time ago: P.B. 12-8-66.
"That's vandalism," said Ruby.
"That's history," said Duarte.
Gran didn't say anything. Her face was wet, but maybe it was only the rain.
Back at the flat, we had hot chocolate, and Gran told us her story.

"I was born here in Graça in 1947. My father was a tram driver, and my mother made dresses for rich ladies. When I was eleven, our teacher gave us the names of some children in Belfast. I chose Peggy because I liked her name. I wrote my first letter with a dictionary, and it took me two weeks. Her answer came a month later. We wrote about everything: school, our families, our dreams. She sent me postcards from her school trips, and I sent her photos and drawings. My English came from her letters." Gran smiled. "Her Portuguese never came from anywhere. She was terrible at languages, but she ran like the wind."
That week I finished my biography project. Claire sent me information, and I wrote it in my best handwriting:

"Margaret Byrne, or Peggy, was born in Belfast in 1947. She was a very fast runner, and she won a lot of races at school. In 1967 she moved to Boston, in the USA, with her family. She studied to be a nurse, and she worked in a big hospital for forty years. She never stopped running. She ran the Boston Marathon nine times. In December she fell on the ice and broke her hip. Now she does her exercises every day, and she walks with a stick. She hates it."
Teacher Sofia gave me a 5, the top mark. "But who is Peggy?" she asked. "A friend of the family," I said, and that was true.
Gran read my project too, and she nodded. Then she got her best pen and some paper. "No phone calls," she said. "We started with letters. We can continue with letters."
She wrote for three evenings. Ruby checked the spelling, but there weren't many mistakes. Then we went with Gran to the post office.
"How much is a stamp for the United States?" she asked. She paid, kissed the envelope and put it in the post box.
Then we waited. One week. Two weeks. Gran checked her letterbox every morning and every afternoon.
The answer came on a sunny Friday at the end of February. It was a blue envelope with an American stamp. Gran opened it in the hall and read it aloud.
"Dear Lurdes, I got your letter. I read it eleven times. I can't travel now, because of my silly hip. So it's your turn. Come to Boston. Love, Peggy. PS: Are you still afraid of aeroplanes?"
Gran folded the letter very carefully.
"I never get on planes," she said. "Never in my life. And I'm not starting now, at seventy-nine."
Then she went into her bedroom and closed the door. A minute later, we heard the music box. The tune played once, then again, then again.

chapters.title: Scones and Shamrocks
paragraphs: For two weeks, Gran didn't answer Peggy's letter. "Planes are for birds," she said. "And birds have got wings."
Ruby had a plan, and her plan's name was Granny Isla.

Granny Isla was Ruby's Scottish grandmother. She was seventy-eight, she had white hair and a purple raincoat, and she flew everywhere. Last year she went to Japan alone. In March she came to Lisbon for a week, and Ruby's family invited Gran, my mum, Duarte and me to afternoon tea.
"Afternoon tea is very British," Ruby explained. "You drink tea with milk and you eat little sandwiches, scones and cakes in the afternoon."
"So it's a lanche," said Duarte.
"It's a lanche with rules," said Ruby.
We arrived early to help Granny Isla in the kitchen. She was making scones and shortbread, a Scottish biscuit with a lot of butter.
"Right," she said. "How much flour have we got?"
Ruby looked in the cupboard. "There's a lot of flour. About a kilo."
"Good. And how many eggs are there?"
"Only one."
"One is enough for the scones. Is there any butter?"
"There isn't much butter. Just a little."
Granny Isla shook her head. "We need some butter for the shortbread. And we haven't got any cream or jam. Duarte, can you go to the shop?"
Duarte went to the shop with ten euros. He came back with butter, cream, jam and two pastéis de nata. "Your change," he said, and he gave Granny Isla twenty cents.
At five o'clock everybody sat at the table. There were cucumber sandwiches, warm scones, shortbread and a big pot of tea. Granny Isla watched us like a teacher in an exam.
"Elbows off the table, young man," she told Duarte. "Knife in your right hand, fork in your left. And we always say please and thank you. 'Can you pass the milk, please?'"
"Can you pass the scones, please?" said Duarte. "All of them?"
"Cream first and then jam, or jam first and then cream?" I asked.
"In England, people argue about that," said Granny Isla. "In Scotland, we just eat them."

Gran and Granny Isla sat next to each other, and soon they were talking like old friends. "I was afraid of planes too," said Granny Isla. "On my first flight, I held the hand of the man next to me for three hours. A stranger! Now he sends me a Christmas card every year." Gran laughed, but she didn't say anything.

A week later, on 17 March, Claire invited us to a St Patrick's Day party at her university. Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland, and on his day, Irish people all over the world wear green and celebrate. There are big parades in Dublin, Belfast, New York and Boston. Everybody at the party was wearing green: green hats, green T-shirts, even green faces. There was Irish music, soda bread and a big pot of Irish stew.
"How much stew did you eat?" I asked Duarte.
"Not much," said Duarte. "Three bowls."
Then Claire took out her phone. "Grandma is at a St Patrick's Day party in Boston too," she said. "She wants to say hello." She looked at Gran. "Is that OK?"
Gran's hands were shaking. Then she nodded.

Claire put the phone against the teapot. On the screen there was an old woman with short white hair, a green hat and very blue eyes. Around her neck, on a thin chain, there was half of a small silver heart.

For a long moment, nobody spoke. The music stopped, and the people at the party went quiet too. Gran's mouth was open, but no words came out. Sixty years were there, in that silence, between a teapot in Lisbon and a phone in Boston.
Then Peggy smiled. "Hello, Lurdes," she said. "You're late."
Gran laughed. "You were on the wrong hill!"
"No, you were on the wrong hill!" Then they both laughed and cried at the same time, and Duarte passed Gran a green napkin.
Suddenly Peggy's face was serious. "Lurdes, I have to ask you something. Why didn't you answer my letters?"
"What letters?"
"From Boston. In 1967. I wrote to you three times. You never answered, so I stopped."
Gran went pale. "Peggy, I didn't get any letters. Not one."
Peggy opened her mouth, and the screen froze. Her face stopped in the middle of a word. Then the screen went black.
Claire stared at her phone. "No battery," she said.
"Three letters," whispered Gran. "Where are they?"

chapters.title: The Sewing Box
paragraphs: It's the Easter holidays, and Gran is making a list. Gran never makes lists. She says lists are for people with bad memories.
This is her list: 1. Find Peggy's letters. 2. Get a passport. 3. Buy a big suitcase. 4. Don't be afraid.
"Avó," I say, "is this a list for a trip?"
"Yes. I'm going to fly to Boston," she says. "In June, after your school finishes. And you're going to come with me, because my English is sixty years old and yours is new."
My mouth opens and closes like a fish.

Mum isn't so sure. She's a nurse, and nurses worry for a living. "OK, Mãe, but you must see the doctor first. You must take your pills every day, and you mustn't forget them in Boston." Then she smiles. "And you must send me photos."
The best news comes from Ruby. "We're going to fly to Boston on 23 June to see my American grandparents. We go every summer. Book the same flight, and we can all travel together!"

Number 2 on the list is harder than it looks, because Gran hasn't got a passport. She doesn't need one for the supermarket. We go to a government office and wait in a queue for an hour and a half. Then a man takes Gran's photo.
"You mustn't smile, please," he says.
Gran looks at me. "Then I'm going to look like a criminal."
She does. The photo is terrible. Gran loves it.

Claire is going to go back to Boston in May, so before she leaves, she gives us a lesson about the USA at the pastelaria. She draws a map on a paper napkin. "The USA is much bigger than Portugal. It has got fifty states. Boston is in Massachusetts, in the north-east. The capital isn't New York, it's Washington, D.C. And the flag has got fifty stars, one for each state, and thirteen stripes."
"Is Boston hotter than Lisbon?" asks Duarte.

"In summer it's hot, but in winter it's much colder than Lisbon. Sometimes the snow is higher than your knees." Claire smiles. "It's one of the oldest cities in the USA, and for my grandma, it's the best city in the world. After Belfast, of course."
But number 1 on the list is the most important. Where are Peggy's letters?
We're sitting on the stairs outside Gran's flat, and we're thinking hard. Ruby is reading Claire's notes. Duarte is eating. I'm looking down at the old letterboxes in the entrance.
"Avó," I say slowly, "in 1967, did your letters come to that letterbox?"

Gran stops. "No. No, they didn't! In 1967 our letterbox was broken. My father never fixed anything. So the postman always left our letters with Dona Graça, across the landing. She was very kind, but she was the most forgetful woman in Graça. Once she forgot her own wedding."
"Dona Graça," says Ruby. "Is she...?"
"Senhora Amélia's mother," says Gran.

We knock on Senhora Amélia's door. Bolacha barks happily when she sees Ruby. Senhora Amélia is seventy-five, and she does everything slowly: she walks slowly, she talks slowly and she thinks carefully before every word. We explain everything, and she listens patiently.
"My mother kept everything," she says at last. "Buttons, string, old keys... Come with me."

In her bedroom there's an old wooden sewing box. It's heavier than it looks. Senhora Amélia opens it carefully. There are buttons of every colour, threads, needles and pins. And under them, at the bottom of the box, there are three thin blue envelopes with American stamps.
"Miss Lurdes Rocha," reads Ruby. The envelopes are still closed, sixty years later.
"Ai, mãe," says Senhora Amélia softly. "Lurdes, I'm so sorry."
Gran takes the letters gently and goes into her flat alone. We wait on the stairs for an hour. Bolacha sleeps on Duarte's feet.

When Gran comes out, her eyes are red, but she's smiling. She reads us one sentence from the third letter: "This is my last letter, because you don't answer, and I'm sad and tired. But one day I'm going to come to Lisbon and knock on your door. Not a hill this time. A door."
Then she says, "Book the tickets, Tomás. And not a word to Peggy or Claire. I want to see Peggy's face when I knock on her door."

In May we say goodbye to Claire at the pastelaria. She's laughing and crying, and she's checking her phone all the time. When she goes to the counter to pay, her phone is on the table, and I see the screen. I'm not spying. Well, only a little. It's an email: "Your booking: Boston (BOS) to Lisbon (LIS). 2 passengers."
Claire comes back and picks up her phone quickly. Her face is red.
"It's for... a friend," she says. "Don't ask."
Two people are flying from Boston to Lisbon. But who are they? And why is Claire's face so red?

chapters.title: Sixty Years and Seven Hours
paragraphs: In June, Lisbon is one big party. For the Santos Populares, the streets of Graça are full of paper flowers and coloured flags, people are grilling sardines on every corner, and every balcony has got a little pot of basil. School finished last week. Today is 23 June, and Gran is going to fly for the first time in her life.
She's wearing her best blue dress, and she's holding her handbag very tightly. Inside the handbag there's her new passport, her pills, Peggy's three letters and the music box.

Duarte isn't coming with us. He's going to a football camp in July, and he's going to water Gran's plants while she's away. He's got her keys. "Don't worry, Senhora Lurdes," he says seriously. "I'm going to look after your flat. And your biscuits."

The airport is bigger and noisier than a football stadium. Ruby is walking quickly, because she flies every year. Gran is walking slowly and nervously, and she's reading every sign aloud. Ruby's mum is explaining the rules. "We must show our passports and our boarding passes. We mustn't leave our bags alone. And we mustn't take big bottles of water or shampoo through security."
At security, a man opens Gran's handbag and takes out a big bottle of shampoo. "Sorry, madam. You mustn't take this on the plane."
"But it's my favourite shampoo!" says Gran, very loudly. Everybody looks at us. I want to disappear.
Then the man finds the music box. "And what's this?"
Gran looks at him proudly. "A present from my best friend. It's sixty years late."
The man smiles and gives it back to her gently.
On the plane Gran sits by the window. "If I'm going to die," she says, "I want to see the ocean first."
"Nobody is going to die, Avó."

When the engines start, she holds my hand tightly. When the plane goes up, she holds Ruby's hand too. Then she holds the hand of the man next to her, a businessman from Texas. He doesn't mind. "First time, ma'am?" he asks kindly.
"Yes," says Gran. "And last time!"

But after an hour, Gran is looking out of the window happily. The clouds are whiter than sheep, and the sea is bigger than she imagined. "It's the most beautiful thing in the world," she says quietly.

Ruby is reading a magazine calmly. "Flying is easier than taking the 28," she says. "Nobody stands on your foot." Gran isn't listening. She's eating her little sandwich slowly, and she's looking at the ocean as if it's a film.

The flight is seven hours long, and it's the longest flight of my life, because Gran tells the businessman everything: the two hills, the music box and the letters in the sewing box. At the end, the businessman is crying into his napkin.
We land in Boston in the afternoon. In Lisbon it's already evening, because Boston is five hours behind. At passport control, a woman in a uniform looks at Gran's passport carefully.
"What's the purpose of your visit, ma'am?"
"I'm going to meet my best friend," says Gran. "For the first time. We started writing letters in 1958."
The woman looks at her for a moment, and then she smiles. "Welcome to the United States."
Ruby's American grandparents are waiting for us with a big sign: WELCOME, LURDES! Gran kisses them both, twice, Portuguese style. They look surprised, but happy.
Then my phone wakes up. There are fifteen messages from Duarte. They all say the same thing: CALL ME. CALL ME NOW.
I call him. His face appears on the screen. There's cream on his nose, and behind him I can see Gran's front door.
"Tomás! Where are you?"
"In Boston, of course. At the airport. Why?"
Duarte turns the phone slowly. On the landing outside Gran's flat, there are two people with suitcases: a young woman with red hair, and an old lady with a stick and a green hat.
"Because they're here," says Duarte. "Peggy and Claire. They landed in Lisbon this morning, and Peggy knocked on your gran's door for ten minutes. I gave them all your gran's biscuits."
Next to me, Gran makes a strange little sound.
On the screen, Peggy looks at the phone and sees Gran. Her blue eyes open wide. "Lurdes?" she says. "Lurdes, where are you?"
Gran's voice is very small. "In Boston, Peggy," she says. "I came to knock on your door."

chapters.title: At the Top of the Hill
paragraphs: For a moment, nobody says anything. Then Peggy starts to laugh. She laughs so much that she has to sit down on Gran's stairs. Claire is laughing too. Then Gran laughs, here in the middle of Boston airport, so loudly that a policeman turns around.
"Sixty years," says Gran, and she wipes her eyes, "and we're on the wrong side of the ocean again!"
"We're the best friends in the world," says Peggy, "and the worst planners."
Then Claire takes the phone. "The doctor says Grandma mustn't fly again for a month," she explains. "This trip was already a big risk."
Gran thinks quickly. "Then I'm going to fly back. Tomorrow. Peggy, listen to me carefully. You mustn't move. Don't go to any door, any hill or any shop. Stay in Lisbon and wait."
"Oh no," says Peggy. "This time I'm going to choose the place. Four o'clock, the day after tomorrow, at the top of your hill. The right hill." She smiles. "And bring the music box."
Changing the tickets is expensive, but Gran pays without a word. "For sixty years I saved money for something important," she says. "I didn't know what it was. Now I know."

So we have one day in Boston, and Ruby's grandparents show us the city. Boston is very different from Lisbon. The streets are wider, the buildings are taller and the cars are much bigger. There's a red line on the pavement called the Freedom Trail, and you can follow it through the city to old churches and houses from American history. Ruby's grandad tells us about the Boston Tea Party. "In 1773, people here were angry about British taxes, so they threw boxes of tea into the harbour."
Ruby looks shocked. "All that tea! Granny Isla is going to cry."

We have lunch in a diner. The pancakes are the biggest pancakes in the world, and the glasses of orange juice are bigger than my head. Gran tastes everything carefully. Then she says, "The food is good and the people are friendly, but our hills are better."
Ruby is staying in Boston for the summer, so we say goodbye at the airport. She hugs Gran tightly. "Call me when you get to the top," she says. "I want to see everything."
The flight home is calm. Gran isn't afraid any more. She's sleeping peacefully next to the window, and she's snoring like the 28 tram on a hill.

Two days later, at a quarter to four, we're climbing the steep streets of Graça. It's hot, and the paper flags from the Santos Populares are still moving in the wind. Gran is holding the music box with both hands. She's walking quickly, then slowly, then quickly again.
Duarte is waiting at the bottom of the steps. "She's up there," he says. "She came at two o'clock. She says she isn't taking any risks this time."

At the top, the pine trees are making shade, the little white chapel is shining in the sun, and all of Lisbon is below us: the red roofs, the river and the castle on its hill. Peggy is sitting on a bench next to the old stone wall. When she sees us, she stands up slowly with her stick.
Gran stops. Peggy stops. They look at each other for a long time.
"You're late," says Peggy.
"Only sixty years," says Gran.
Then they're hugging, and they're laughing and crying, and nobody else can say a word. Duarte is crying too. "It's the sun," he says. "It's in my eyes."
When they sit down, Gran opens the music box and takes out the little envelope. Her hands are shaking, so she gives it to me. "You read it, Tomás. Your English is new."
I open it carefully. Inside, there's a letter and half of a small silver heart.
"Dear Lurdes," I read. "If you're reading this, we're together at last. This is half of my heart. I've got the other half, and I'm going to wear it until I see you. Your friend forever, Peggy."
Peggy takes the chain from her neck. Gran puts the two halves together, and they fit perfectly. Then she opens the music box, and the old tune plays again over the roofs of Lisbon.
There's one more thing I must do. "Avó," I say quietly, "in September, when you asked about my pocket, I lied. It wasn't my phone."
Gran laughs. "I know, Tomás. You're a terrible liar. You always look at your shoes."
Then Peggy takes a key out of her bag, turns to the old stone wall and, very carefully, scratches new letters next to the old ones: L.R. + P.B.
Ruby is watching everything on my phone from Boston. "That's vandalism!" she shouts.
"That's history," says Duarte. "Now, who's hungry?"

fichas.title: Behind the Wardrobe

reading.title: Behind the Wardrobe
text: It's Saturday morning. Tomás, Duarte and Ruby are helping Tomás's gran, Avó Lurdes, in her flat in Graça, Lisbon. The painters are coming on Monday, so Gran needs an empty hall.

Now everybody is working. Duarte is sweeping the floor, but he's eating a biscuit at the same time. Ruby is putting old books into boxes. Gran is standing in the middle of the hall like a football coach. She isn't working. She's giving orders.
On Saturday mornings, Gran usually sits in her armchair and listens to the radio. Today she isn't sitting and she isn't singing. She's nervous.

Ruby holds up a blue scarf. "Senhora Lurdes, is this yours?" she asks in English. "No, it isn't mine. It's my sister's," Gran answers, in perfect English. "From letters," she says, when Ruby asks where she learnt it.

The children push the wardrobe and an old tin box falls from the top. There are postcards everywhere: Edinburgh Castle, Tower Bridge in London, a castle in Cardiff and City Hall in Belfast. They all end with the words "Your friend forever, Peggy." Gran takes them and locks them in her bedroom.

Behind the wardrobe there's one more postcard, with no stamp. It's from 1966. Peggy is writing to Lurdes: she waited for her at the top of her hill, and a man called Mr Costa is keeping a present for her at his shop, Casa Costa. The shop still exists, but it's closing down on 31 October.
Tomás puts the postcard in his pocket. Then Gran's door opens. "Tomás, what have you got in your pocket?"

reading.title: Everything Must Go
text: On Monday after school, Tomás, Ruby and Duarte take the 28 tram from Largo da Graça. The tram is full of tourists, and everybody is taking photos. The children get off in Rua da Conceição, but they're lost. They ask a man for directions. "Go straight on. Turn left at the church. Casa Costa is on the right, opposite the bakery."
Casa Costa is dark and quiet. Clocks are ticking on every wall. Ruby asks the price of a gramophone. "Two hundred and fifty euros," says Senhor Costa. "That's very expensive!" says Ruby.

Senhor Costa's father wrote everything in a notebook. The notebook says: a music box, paid, for Miss Lurdes Rocha. But last week Dona Fátima from the Feira da Ladra bought everything in the special cupboard.

On Saturday the children go to the flea market. It's open on Tuesdays and Saturdays. The music box is there, with two silver birds on the lid. It costs eighty euros, and an American girl wants it too. The children have only thirty-six euros seventy.

So this week they're working hard. Duarte is washing cars, Ruby is walking Senhora Amélia's dog, and Tomás is carrying shopping bags for old ladies. On Friday they've got eighty euros and thirty cents.
On Saturday they run to the market, but the music box isn't there. A young woman with red hair and a green coat is getting on the tram, and she's holding the box.

reading.title: A Guest for Thanksgiving
text: Ruby's mum is American, so her family celebrates Thanksgiving. It's an American holiday on the fourth Thursday of November. Families have a big dinner together, eat turkey and say what they're thankful for.
Tomás, his mum, Gran and Duarte are at Ruby's flat. Ruby's dad is mashing potatoes and singing. Ruby's mum is taking a huge turkey out of the oven. Duarte is tasting everything.
"Senhora Lurdes, this is your seat," says Ruby. "And this one is mine. Duarte, that chair isn't yours, it's my dad's!"
There's turkey, mashed potatoes, sweet potatoes and a red sauce made with cranberries. "Red jam with meat?" whispers Duarte. Then he tries it, and he has three spoonfuls.

There's one more guest: a student from Boston. When she arrives, the children can't believe it. It's the woman with red hair! Her name is Claire. "I know you three," she says. "You were running after my tram!"

After dinner, everybody says what they're thankful for. Claire is thankful because she found a present for her grandmother. Sixty years ago, her grandmother came to Lisbon to meet her pen pal, but her friend never came. Claire opens the music box, and a sad tune fills the room.
Gran's face is white. "What is your grandmother's name?" she asks.
"Peggy. When she was a girl in Belfast, she was Peggy Byrne."
Gran stands up. "That's impossible. Peggy Byrne is dead."

reading.title: Gone Away
text: "Dead?" said Claire. "No! My grandmother isn't dead. She's seventy-nine and she's very much alive."
Gran sat down again. "But in 1967 I wrote to her in Belfast, and my letter came back. On the envelope there were two words in red ink: GONE AWAY."
Ruby's mum explained: "Gone away" doesn't mean dead. The post office writes it on a letter when the person moved house. In 1967, Peggy's family moved from Belfast to Boston.
Then Tomás gave Gran the postcard from behind the wardrobe. He was nervous. "I'm sorry, Avó," he said. Gran read it twice. She didn't say anything for a long time.
Claire gave Gran the music box. Inside the lid there was a small envelope: "For Lurdes. Open it when we meet. P." Gran didn't open it.
"Why don't you call Peggy?" Tomás asked in December. "Because she didn't come," said Gran. "On 12 August 1966, I waited at the castle from four o'clock until seven. I was nineteen. She wasn't there."
January was cold and wet. It rained for eleven days. Duarte played in a football match in the rain, slipped in the mud and hurt his ankle. He was on crutches for three weeks.

For a school project, Tomás chose Peggy. Claire told the children about her. Peggy was born in Belfast in 1947, and she was the fastest runner in her school. Then Claire showed them a photo of Lurdes at twelve. Lurdes was next to a small white chapel, and the castle was behind her, far away. She wasn't at the castle. She was on a different hill!

reading.title: The Wrong Hill
text: Gran looked at the photo and put her hand over her mouth. "Senhora do Monte," she whispered. "My hill. I sent her this photo when I was twelve. In 1966 I didn't think about the photo. Foreigners always go to the castle, so I went to the castle."

Then she put on her coat. "I want to go there now." It was the worst storm of the winter. The wind was strong and the rain was heavy, but Gran walked up the hill faster than all of them. At the top, under the green moss on an old stone wall, they found small letters: P.B. 12-8-66.
"That's vandalism," said Ruby. "That's history," said Duarte.

Back at the flat, Gran told them her story. She was born in Graça in 1947. Her father was a tram driver. When she was eleven, her teacher gave the class the names of some children in Belfast, and she chose Peggy. She wrote her first letter with a dictionary. It took her two weeks!

Tomás wrote Peggy's biography for his English project. Peggy moved to Boston in 1967. She became a nurse and ran the Boston Marathon nine times. In December she fell on the ice and broke her hip. Now she walks with a stick.

Gran wrote a long letter to Peggy, and they posted it. Two weeks later, the answer came: "I can't travel now, because of my hip. So it's your turn. Come to Boston. Are you still afraid of aeroplanes?"
"I never get on planes," said Gran. "Never in my life."

reading.title: Scones and Shamrocks
text: In March, Ruby's Scottish grandmother, Granny Isla, came to Lisbon, and Ruby's family invited everybody to afternoon tea. "You drink tea with milk and you eat little sandwiches, scones and cakes," Ruby explained.

In the kitchen, Granny Isla made scones and shortbread. "How much flour have we got?" she asked. "There's a lot of flour," said Ruby. "How many eggs are there?" "Only one." "Is there any butter?" "There isn't much butter." "We need some butter, and we haven't got any cream or jam." Duarte went to the shop.
At the table, Granny Isla taught them British table manners. "Elbows off the table. Knife in your right hand, fork in your left. And say please and thank you."
Granny Isla wasn't afraid of planes. "On my first flight, I was very scared," she told Gran. "I held the hand of the man next to me for three hours!"

On 17 March, Claire invited them to a St Patrick's Day party. Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland. On his day, people wear green and there are parades in Dublin, Belfast, New York and Boston. At the party there was Irish music, soda bread and Irish stew.

Then Claire called her grandmother in Boston. Peggy was on the screen, with a green hat and half of a silver heart on a chain. "Hello, Lurdes. You're late." The two old friends laughed. But then Peggy asked, "Why didn't you answer my three letters from Boston?" Gran didn't get any letters! And then the phone died.

reading.title: The Sewing Box
text: It's the Easter holidays, and Gran is making a list: 1. Find Peggy's letters. 2. Get a passport. 3. Buy a big suitcase. 4. Don't be afraid.
"I'm going to fly to Boston in June," she says. "And you're going to come with me, Tomás." Tomás's mum is a nurse. "You must see the doctor first," she says. "And you mustn't forget your pills."
Gran hasn't got a passport, so they go to a government office. A man takes her photo. "You mustn't smile, please." "Then I'm going to look like a criminal," says Gran.

Before Claire goes back to Boston, she teaches the children about the USA. "The USA is much bigger than Portugal. It has got fifty states. The capital is Washington, D.C. The flag has got fifty stars and thirteen stripes. In winter, Boston is much colder than Lisbon."

But where are Peggy's letters? Tomás has an idea. In 1967, Gran's letterbox was broken, so the postman left her letters with the neighbour, Dona Graça. She was the most forgetful woman in Graça. Her daughter, Senhora Amélia, opens her mother's old sewing box. Under the buttons and needles, there are three blue envelopes from America. They're still closed!
In the third letter, Peggy wrote: "One day I'm going to come to Lisbon and knock on your door." Gran smiles. "Book the tickets, Tomás. And don't tell Peggy or Claire."
In May, Tomás sees an email on Claire's phone: "Boston to Lisbon. 2 passengers." Claire's face is red. "Don't ask," she says.

reading.title: Sixty Years and Seven Hours
text: It's 23 June, and Gran is going to fly for the first time in her life. Duarte isn't going. He's going to water Gran's plants.

The airport is bigger and noisier than a football stadium. Ruby walks quickly, because she flies every year. Gran walks slowly and nervously. Ruby's mum explains the rules: "We must show our passports. We mustn't leave our bags alone. And we mustn't take big bottles of water or shampoo through security."

At security, a man finds Gran's big bottle of shampoo. "Sorry, madam. You mustn't take this on the plane." "But it's my favourite shampoo!" says Gran loudly. Then he finds the music box. "A present from my best friend," says Gran proudly. "It's sixty years late." The man smiles and gives it back to her gently.
When the plane goes up, Gran holds Tomás's hand tightly. But after an hour, she's looking out of the window happily. "The sea is bigger than I imagined," she says.
The flight is seven hours long. In Boston, a woman at passport control asks, "What's the purpose of your visit?" "I'm going to meet my best friend," says Gran. "For the first time."

Then Tomás calls Duarte. Behind Duarte, on the landing outside Gran's flat, there are two people with suitcases: Claire and Peggy! They landed in Lisbon that morning. Peggy wanted to surprise Lurdes, and Lurdes wanted to surprise Peggy.
"Lurdes, where are you?" asks Peggy.
"In Boston, Peggy. I came to knock on your door."

fichas.title: At the Top of the Hill
fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 9 · Grammar: connectors (and, but, because, so); comparatives and superlatives; going to

reading.title: At the Top of the Hill
text: Peggy and Lurdes laugh and laugh. "Sixty years," says Gran, "and we're on the wrong side of the ocean again!" Peggy mustn't fly again for a month, so Gran is going to fly back to Lisbon. "Four o'clock, the day after tomorrow, at the top of your hill," says Peggy.

Changing the tickets is expensive, but Gran pays without a word. They have one day in Boston. The streets are wider, the buildings are taller and the cars are bigger than in Lisbon. They follow the Freedom Trail, a red line on the pavement. Ruby's grandad tells them about the Boston Tea Party: in 1773, people were angry about British taxes, so they threw boxes of tea into the harbour.
In a diner, the pancakes are the biggest pancakes in the world. "The food is good and the people are friendly," says Gran, "but our hills are better."
Two days later, they climb to Senhora do Monte. Peggy is sitting on a bench next to the old stone wall. "You're late," says Peggy. "Only sixty years," says Gran. They hug, and everybody cries.
Gran opens the music box and Tomás reads Peggy's old letter: "This is half of my heart. I've got the other half." Peggy takes her chain, and the two halves fit perfectly.
Then Tomás tells Gran the truth about his pocket in September. Gran laughs. "I know. You're a terrible liar, because you always look at your shoes."
Peggy scratches new letters on the wall next to the old ones: L.R. + P.B. "That's history," says Duarte. "Now, who's hungry?"

sebenta.html:
Verb to be (ser / estar)

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion / short answer
I am (I'm)
you are (you're)
he / she / it is (he's)
we / you / they are (we're)		 I am not (I'm not)
you aren't
he / she / it isn't
we / you / they aren't		 Are you Portuguese? – Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
Is she tall? – Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.

Have got (ter)

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion / short answer
I / you / we / they have got ('ve got)
he / she / it has got ('s got)		 I haven't got
he hasn't got		 Have you got a pet? – Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
Has he got a bike? – Yes, he has.

There is / There are (há)

There is + singular (There is a park near my house.) · There are + plural (There are two cinemas.) · Negative: There isn't / There aren't · Questions: Is there a bank here? – Yes, there is. · Are there any shops? – No, there aren't.

Present Simple and adverbs of frequency

FormUseExamples
I / you / we / they play
he / she / it plays (watches, goes, studies)
neg.: don't / doesn't + verb
quest.: Do / Does + subject + verb?		 • habits and routines (rotinas)
• facts (factos)
• likes and dislikes		 I get up at 7 o'clock.
She goes to school by bus.
He doesn't like fish.
Does she play tennis? – Yes, she does.

Adverbs of frequency: always (100%) · usually · often · sometimes · never (0%). They go before the verb but after to be: I always have breakfast. / I am never late.

Can (capacidade e pedidos)

can / can't + verb (no -s, no to): I can swim. · She can't drive. · Can you play the guitar? – Yes, I can. · Can I open the window, please?

Articles and plurals

  • a + consonant sound (a dog, a uniform) · an + vowel sound (an apple, an hour) · the = something specific (the sun, the book on the table).
  • Plural: -s (cats) · -es after -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o (buses, watches, tomatoes) · consonant + y → -ies (babies) · -f / -fe → -ves (leaves, knives).
  • Irregular: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice, sheep → sheep, fish → fish.

Possessive case ('s)

singular + 's: Ana's bag · my brother's room · plural ending in -s + ': my parents' car · irregular plural + 's: the children's toys. Possessive determiners: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.

sebenta.title: Present Continuous
sebenta.html:
We use the Present Continuous for actions that are happening now, at the moment of speaking (ações a decorrer agora).

Form: to be + verb-ing

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion
I am playing (I'm playing)
you are playing (you're playing)
he / she / it is playing (he's playing)
we / you / they are playing (they're playing)		 I am not playing (I'm not)
you aren't playing
he / she / it isn't playing
we / you / they aren't playing		 Am I playing?
Are you playing?
Is he / she / it playing?
Are we / you / they playing?

Short answers: Are you listening? – Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. · Is she sleeping? – Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. · Are they working? – Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.

Wh- questions: What are you doing? · Where is he going? · Why are they laughing? · Who is she talking to?

Use

UseExamples
actions happening now, at this momentLook! The dog is eating my sandwich.
I'm doing my homework at the moment.
temporary situations (situações temporárias, around now)We're staying at my grandmother's this week.
She's learning to swim this summer.
household chores and activities in progress (tarefas domésticas)Mum is cooking dinner and Dad is washing the car.
I'm tidying my room.

Time expressions: now · right now · at the moment · today · this week · this morning · Look! · Listen! · Be quiet!

Spelling of the -ing form

RuleExamples
most verbs: add -ingplay → playing · read → reading · go → going · study → studying
verbs ending in -e: drop the e, add -ingmake → making · dance → dancing · write → writing · have → having
one vowel + one consonant (short verbs): double the consonantrun → running · swim → swimming · sit → sitting · shop → shopping · get → getting
verbs ending in -ie: -ie → -yinglie → lying · die → dying
Don't double the consonant when the verb ends in -w, -x, -y or has two vowels: snowing, fixing, playing, eating, raining.

Household chores (tarefas domésticas) – useful verbs

make the bed · tidy the room · do the washing-up · lay / clear the table · take out the rubbish · do the laundry · vacuum the floor · water the plants · walk the dog · feed the cat · sweep the floor · dust the furniture

What is everybody doing? – Tom is taking out the rubbish, Lucy is laying the table and I'm feeding the cat.

Form: verb / verb + -s (he, she, it)

Stative verbs – verbs we don't use in the continuous

Some verbs describe states (feelings, thoughts, possession), not actions. We use them in the Present Simple, even when we mean "now":

sebenta.title: Past Simple: regular verbs
sebenta.html:
We use the Past Simple for finished actions in the past (ações acabadas). The form is the same for all persons.

Form

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion

After didn't and Did, the verb goes back to the base form: She didn't like it (not didn't liked) · Did you walk home? (not Did you walked).

RuleExamples

consonant + -y: -y → -iedstudy → studied · try → tried · carry → carried · cry → cried

First we went to the zoo. Then we had a picnic. Suddenly it started to rain, so we ran to the car. Finally, we got home at 7.

A short biography

Amália Rodrigues was born in Lisbon in 1920. She started singing when she was a teenager and became famous all over the world. She made many records and films, and she died in 1999.

sebenta.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
sebenta.html:
Countable nouns (contáveis)Uncountable nouns (incontáveis)
We can count them: one apple, two apples.
They have a singular and a plural.
Singular: a / an + noun (an egg, a banana).		 We cannot count them – no plural, no a / an.
We use a container or a measure: a glass of water, a bottle of milk, a piece of cake, a slice of bread, a cup of tea, a kilo of rice, a bar of chocolate, a packet of crisps.
apple · egg · sandwich · biscuit · carrot · tomato · burger · coin · shop · ticket · bike · friend water · milk · juice · bread · cheese · butter · rice · pasta · meat · sugar · salt · fruit · money · time · music · homework · information · advice · furniture
Careful: money, bread, fruit, homework, furniture, information, advice are uncountable in English: I need some money (not a money) · We have a lot of homework (not homeworks). Uncountable nouns take a singular verb: Milk is good for you.

Some / any

WordUseExamples
someaffirmative sentences (plural countable + uncountable)
offers and requests (Would you like…? Can I have…?)		There are some biscuits. · I've got some money.
Would you like some tea? · Can I have some water?
anynegative sentences and questionsThere isn't any milk. · We haven't got any eggs.
Are there any apples? · Have you got any brothers?
no= not any (with an affirmative verb)There's no bread. = There isn't any bread.

Much / many / a lot of

WordUseExamples
many+ plural countable nouns (negatives and questions)I haven't got many friends here. · Are there many shops?
much+ uncountable nouns (negatives and questions)There isn't much juice. · Do you drink much milk?
a lot of / lots of+ countable and uncountable (mainly affirmative)She eats a lot of fruit. · We've got lots of books.

How much…? / How many…?

QuestionAnswer
How many eggs do we need? (countable)Six. / A lot. / Not many.
How much sugar do you want? (uncountable)Two spoons. / A little. / Not much.
How much is this T-shirt? / How much does it cost? (price)It's £12.50. / It costs twelve pounds fifty.

sebenta.title: Comparatives and superlatives
sebenta.html:
Comparative (+ than): compares two things (mais … do que). Superlative (the + …): one thing in a group of three or more (o mais …).

AdjectiveComparativeSuperlative
short (1 syllable): tall, fast, cheap, oldtaller, faster, cheaperthe tallest, the fastest, the cheapest
ending in -e: nice, large, safenicer, larger, saferthe nicest, the largest, the safest
one vowel + one consonant: big, hot, thin, fatbigger, hotter, thinnerthe biggest, the hottest, the thinnest
ending in -y: happy, easy, funny, healthyhappier, easier, funnierthe happiest, the easiest, the funniest
long (2+ syllables): beautiful, expensive, dangerous, interestingmore beautiful, more expensivethe most beautiful, the most expensive
irregular: good, bad, farbetter, worse, farther / furtherthe best, the worst, the farthest / furthest

Comparative: … than

  • A car is faster than a bike. · Maths is more difficult than English. · My sister is older than me.
  • less … than (menos … do que): This phone is less expensive than that one.
  • much / a lot + comparative: Lisbon is much bigger than Évora. · a bit + comparative: He is a bit taller than me.

Superlative: the … in / of

  • Rita is the tallest girl in the class. · The Nile is the longest river in the world. · It was the best day of my life.
  • in + place or group (in the class, in Portugal, in my family) · of + period (of the year, of my life).

As … as (tão … como)

StructureExamples
as + adjective + as → the sameTom is as tall as his dad. · Today is as cold as yesterday.
not as + adjective + as → lessA bus isn't as fast as a train. (= A train is faster than a bus.)

Sport and health – comparing

Swimming is healthier than playing video games. · Football is the most popular sport in Portugal. · Running is as good as cycling for your heart. · Fruit is better than sweets. · Smoking is the worst habit.

Typical mistakes: more big → bigger · more better → better · the most tallest → the tallest · taller that me → taller than me · the best of the class → the best in the class · expensiver → more expensive.

sebenta.html:
Subject pronounObject pronounPossessive determiner (+ noun)Possessive pronoun (no noun)

youyouyour bikeyours
hehimhis bikehis
sheherher bikehers
ititits wheel–
weusour bikesours
youyouyour bikesyours
theythemtheir bikestheirs

Object pronouns (pronomes complemento)

They come after the verb or after a preposition (to, for, with, at, about). They replace the person or thing that receives the action.

UseExamples
after a verbI like Ana. → I like her. · Can you help me? · We saw them at the park. · Don't eat it!
after a prepositionThis present is for you. · Come with us! · Listen to him. · Look at it.
in short answers and with tooWho's there? – It's me. · I love pizza. – Me too!
Subject or object? She phoned him (she = who does it; him = who receives it). Not Her phoned he. · My friend and I went out (subject) / He came with my friend and me (object).

Possessive pronouns (pronomes possessivos)

They stand alone – there is no noun after them. They mean "determiner + noun": mine = my + noun.

Possessive determiner + nounPossessive pronoun (no noun)
This is my jacket.This jacket is mine.
Is that your phone?Is that phone yours?
Those are their seats.Those seats are theirs.
Her house is big. Our house is small.Hers is big. Ours is small.

Whose…? asks about possession: Whose bag is this? – It's mine. / It's Pedro's. Also: a friend of mine (um amigo meu).

Don't confuse: its (possessive: The dog wagged its tail) and it's (= it is: It's raining) · their (their car), there (over there) and they're (= they are) · your (your book) and you're (= you are).

Summary

I gave him my pen because his was broken, and he gave me his ruler. Now this pen is his and that ruler is mine!

sebenta.title: Going to: future plans
sebenta.html:
We use be going to + verb to talk about plans and intentions for the future (o que tencionamos fazer) and to make predictions when we can see evidence now.

Form: to be + going to + verb

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion
I am going to visit (I'm going to)
you are going to visit
he / she / it is going to visit
we / you / they are going to visit		 I am not going to visit
you aren't going to visit
he / she / it isn't going to visit
we / you / they aren't going to visit		 Am I going to visit…?
Are you going to visit…?
Is he / she / it going to visit…?
Are we / you / they going to visit…?

Short answers: Are you going to study tonight? – Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. · Is it going to rain? – Yes, it is. / No, it isn't.

Use

UseExamples
plans and intentions (decided before speaking)We're going to visit Scotland next summer.
I'm going to be a vet when I grow up.
She isn't going to come to the party.
predictions with evidence (we can see it's going to happen)Look at those black clouds! It's going to rain.
Careful! You're going to fall.

Time expressions: tomorrow · tonight · next week / month / year / summer · on Saturday · at the weekend · this evening · in two days · soon · after school

Wh- questions

QuestionAnswer
What are you going to do this weekend?I'm going to go to the beach.
Where is he going to stay?He's going to stay in a hotel.
When are they going to leave?They're going to leave on Friday.
How are you going to travel?We're going to travel by plane.
Who are you going to go with?With my cousins.
go and come: we often say I'm going to the cinema (Present Continuous) instead of I'm going to go to the cinema. Both are correct.

Holidays and travel – useful language

Transport: by car / bus / train / plane / boat / bike · on foot. Places to stay: a hotel, a campsite, a youth hostel, my grandparents' house. Activities: go sightseeing, go swimming, sunbathe, take photos, visit a museum, try the local food, buy souvenirs.

Next summer we're going to go to Madeira. We're going to fly from Porto and stay at a campsite. I'm going to go swimming every day and my sister is going to take lots of photos. We aren't going to take the dog – he's going to stay with my aunt.

Typical mistakes: I going to play → I am going to play · She is going to plays → She is going to play · We go to visit Rome next week → We are going to visit Rome next week.

sebenta.title: Must and mustn't
sebenta.html:
Must and mustn't are modal verbs: they are followed by the base form of the verb (no to), they have no -s in the 3rd person and they make questions without do.

FormUseExamples
must + verb
I / you / he / she / it / we / they must go		obligation (é obrigatório / é preciso), rules, strong adviceYou must wear a helmet on a bike.
Students must be quiet in the library.
I must do more exercise.
mustn't (must not) + verbprohibition (é proibido / não podes)You mustn't run near the pool.
We mustn't use our phones in class.
You mustn't eat so many sweets.
Must + subject + verb?questions (not very common)Must I finish it today? – Yes, you must. / No, you needn't.
mustn't ≠ don't have to. You mustn't go = it is forbidden (não podes ir). You don't have to go = it isn't necessary (não precisas de ir). You mustn't touch the paintings. · You don't have to pay – the museum is free.

Must and have to

ModalMeaningExamples
mustthe speaker thinks it is necessary (I decide)I must tidy my room – it's a mess.
have to / has toa rule or an external obligation (someone else decides)We have to wear a uniform at school. · She has to get up at 6.
don't / doesn't have tono obligation (não é preciso)You don't have to come if you're tired.

Rules and signs

SignWhat it means
NO SMOKINGYou mustn't smoke here.
KEEP OFF THE GRASSYou mustn't walk on the grass.
FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTYou must fasten your seat belt.
TICKETS ONLYYou must have a ticket.
NO PHOTOSYou mustn't take photos.

Other modals you know

ModalMeaningExamples
can / can'tability; permissionShe can ski. · Can I go to the toilet?
couldpolite requestCould you open the window, please?
should / shouldn'tadvice (deves / não deves)You should see a doctor. · You shouldn't eat so fast.

sebenta.title: Adverbs of manner
sebenta.html:
Adverbs of manner say how we do something (como fazemos algo). An adjective describes a noun (a slow car); an adverb describes a verb (he drives slowly).

RuleExamples
most adjectives: add -lyslow → slowly · quick → quickly · quiet → quietly · careful → carefully · bad → badly
adjectives ending in -y: -y → -ilyhappy → happily · easy → easily · noisy → noisily · angry → angrily
adjectives ending in -le: -le → -lyterrible → terribly · gentle → gently · simple → simply
adjectives ending in -ic: add -allyfantastic → fantastically · automatic → automatically
irregulargood → well · fast → fast · hard → hard · late → late · early → early
Adjective (describes a noun)Adverb (describes a verb)
She is a careful driver.She drives carefully.
He is a good singer.He sings well.
They are fast runners.They run fast.
The children were quiet.The children played quietly.
The adverb usually goes after the verb or after the object: He speaks English fluently. (not He speaks fluently English). Hardly ≠ hard: hardly = almost not (I hardly know him); he works hard = he works a lot.

11Connectors: and, but, because, so

ConnectorUseExamples
and (e)adds information; joins two similar ideasI like tennis and basketball. · We went to the beach and we swam all afternoon.
but (mas)contrast; two different or opposite ideasThe hotel was nice, but the food was terrible. · I can swim, but I can't dive.
because (porque)gives a reason; answers Why…?I stayed at home because I was ill. · Why are you late? – Because I missed the bus.
so (por isso)gives a result or consequenceI was ill, so I stayed at home. · It was very hot, so we went for a swim.
because and so are opposites: It was raining, so we didn't go out. (rain → result) · We didn't go out because it was raining. (result ← reason). Don't use both together: because it rained so we stayed.

Other useful connectors

or (ou): Do you want tea or coffee? · also / too (também): I also play the piano. · She likes it too. · then (depois): We had lunch, then we visited the castle. · when (quando): I was happy when I saw the sea.

Last summer we went to Peniche because my uncle lives there. The weather was great, so we went to the beach every day. I surfed and played volleyball, but my brother just slept!

A day in the past – model text

Last Saturday I woke up late. I had breakfast and then I went to the park with my friends. We played football and ate ice cream. In the afternoon it rained, so we stayed at home and watched a film. I didn't do my homework – I forgot! In the evening my grandparents came to dinner and my mum made a chocolate cake. It was a great day.

Study tip: learn the irregular verbs in small groups of 5 or 6 a week. Say them aloud (go – went, see – saw…) and write one sentence with each verb.

Useful phrases

SituationPhrases
Asking for and giving directionsExcuse me, how do I get to the station? · Where's the nearest bank? · Go straight on. · Turn left / right at the traffic lights. · Take the first / second turning on the left. · It's on the corner / opposite the cinema / next to the bakery / between the bank and the post office. · It's about five minutes on foot.
TransportWhich bus goes to the centre? · A single / return ticket to Oxford, please. · What time does the next train leave? · Does this bus stop at the museum? · Get on / get off at the third stop.
ShoppingCan I help you? – I'm just looking, thanks. · How much is this? / How much are these? · It's too expensive / too big. · Have you got a smaller size? · Can I pay by card? · Here you are. – Thank you. Here's your change.
Talking about the weatherWhat's the weather like? · It's sunny / cloudy / rainy / windy / foggy / snowy. · It's hot / warm / cold / freezing. · It's 25 degrees. · It's raining / snowing. · What was the weather like? – It was terrible!
Talking about holidaysWhere did you go on holiday? · Who did you go with? · How did you get there? · Where did you stay? · What did you do? · Did you have a good time? – Yes, it was amazing! / No, it was boring. · The best part was… · Next summer I'm going to…
Writing an emailHi Jack, · Thanks for your email. · How are you? · Guess what! · Write back soon! · Love, / See you soon, / Bye for now,
